lesson.title: Writing Change as a Ratio
lesson.summary: Presents Leibniz's dy over dx notation as a ratio of infinitesimal changes that always names its variables, worked through a circle area example to show why it suits related quantities.
lesson.body:
Leibniz notation, developed by Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz, writes the derivative of y with respect to x as dy divided by dx. The symbols d y and d x are meant to evoke an infinitesimally small change in y and the infinitesimally small change in x that produced it, a direct echo of the difference quotient [f(x + h) minus f(x)] divided by h with h shrunk down toward, but never reaching, 0. Unlike prime notation, this form always states explicitly which variable is changing with respect to which other variable, which matters as soon as a problem involves more than two related quantities.

The instruction form of this notation, d divided by dx applied to an expression in parentheses or brackets, means "differentiate what follows with respect to x," and is especially useful for differentiating an expression on the spot without first giving it a name like y or f. To evaluate a derivative at a specific input, Leibniz notation places a vertical bar after the expression with the input value written below it, such as dy divided by dx, evaluated at x equals a.

Here is a worked example using a different setting than the polynomial cases seen so far: the area of a circle as a function of its radius, A = pi times r squared. Using the limit definition with radius as the variable, dA divided by dr equals the limit as h approaches 0 of [pi times (r + h) squared minus pi times r squared] divided by h. Expanding (r + h) squared gives r squared plus 2rh plus h squared, so pi times that is pi r squared plus 2 pi r h plus pi h squared. Subtracting pi r squared leaves 2 pi r h plus pi h squared, and dividing by h gives 2 pi r plus pi h. As h approaches 0, this becomes 2 pi r. So dA divided by dr equals 2 pi r.

Evaluate at r = 3: dA divided by dr, at r = 3, equals 2 pi times 3, which is 6 pi, approximately 18.85. This says that when a circle's radius is 3 units, its area is growing at a rate of 6 pi square units for every additional unit of radius, information the notation dA divided by dr communicates directly, since both the changing quantity, area, and what it is changing with respect to, radius, are written into the symbol itself.

One reason Leibniz notation has such staying power is that dy and dx, while not officially separate numbers within this definition, behave as if they can be handled individually in later techniques, such as separating variables in certain differential equations. That informal flexibility, treating dy divided by dx almost like an actual fraction, is only ever a convenience built on top of the rigorous limit definition, never a replacement for it, but it is a convenience Leibniz notation offers uniquely.

This built in bookkeeping is why Leibniz notation becomes indispensable once calculus moves into topics like related rates, where several quantities change together and you need to track exactly which variable each rate is measured against, and the chain rule, where derivatives of nested functions are combined by what looks almost like canceling fractions, dy divided by du times du divided by dx equals dy divided by dx. That structure is only visible in Leibniz's form, which is part of why it survives alongside prime notation rather than being replaced by it.
